question: What does the international standard for the operation of aircraft (its operating annex) contain?

options.text: The procedures air traffic controllers use to separate traffic in controlled airspace
The design standards for aeroplanes in the transport category
The rules of the air that apply to all flights over the high seas
Standards for issuing an AOC for international commercial air transport

explanation: The operating annex contains the international standards and recommended practices that apply to issuing an air operator certificate (AOC) for international commercial air transport. Design standards and air traffic procedures are in other documents.

question: The international operating annex is published in three parts. What does Part 1 cover?

options.text: Helicopters in international commercial air transport
Aeroplanes in international commercial air transport
All aircraft engaged in aerial work and training
Aeroplanes in general aviation

explanation: Part 1 covers aeroplanes in international commercial air transport, Part 2 aeroplanes in general aviation, and Part 3 helicopters in international commercial air transport.

question: Which part of the international operating annex covers helicopters in international commercial air transport?

options.text: Part 3
Part 4
Part 1
Part 2

explanation: Part 3 covers helicopters used in international commercial air transport. Parts 1 and 2 cover aeroplanes.

question: What term does the international operating standard use for the commander of a flight?

options.text: Aircraft master
Senior flight officer
Pilot-in-command
Captain

explanation: The international standard still uses the term pilot-in-command (PIC); regional rules call the same person the commander.

question: An operator flies international services. Whose laws must its aeroplanes and crews comply with?

options.text: Only the laws of the State of Registry
Only the laws of the State of the Operator
Those of the foreign States as well as the State of the Operator
Only the laws of the State in which the flight departs

explanation: Operators in international service are subject to the laws of foreign States as well as those of the State of the Operator (and the State of Registry, if different).

question: Who must ensure that all employees, wherever they are, comply with the laws of the State they are operating in?

options.text: The operator
The State in which each employee holds a licence
Each employee alone
The State of Registry

explanation: It is incumbent on the operator to ensure that all employees, anywhere in the world, comply with the laws of the State in which they are operating or based.

question: Which rules must pilots be familiar with for the airspace they will fly in?

options.text: Only the operator's own procedures
Only the rules of the State of Registry of the aircraft
Only the rules of the air of the State that issued their licence
The rules of the air and ATS regulations there

explanation: Pilots are to be conversant with the rules of the air and the ATS regulations for the airspace in which they will be flying.

question: What is operational control?

options.text: Planning the crew roster for the following month
Authority over starting, continuing, diverting or ending a flight
Controlling the aircraft's flight path by hand or autopilot
Separating aircraft in controlled airspace

explanation: Operational control is the exercise of authority over the initiation, continuation, diversion or termination of a flight, in the interest of safety and of regularity and efficiency.

question: Who holds responsibility for operational control?

options.text: The aircraft's approved maintenance organisation
The State of the Operator
The air traffic control unit
The operator or its representative

explanation: The operator, or a designated representative, has responsibility for operational control.

question: To whom may responsibility for operational control be delegated?

options.text: To the ground handling agent at each station
The PIC, and exceptionally a dispatcher
To any member of the crew
To the air traffic controller in whose area the aircraft is flying

explanation: Operational control may only be delegated to the pilot-in-command, and exceptionally to a flight operations officer or dispatcher if the approved method of supervision uses such staff.

question: Before an air operator certificate is issued, what must the operator show?

options.text: That it is safe as well as viable
Only that it has enough money to operate for a year
Only that its pilots hold licences from the same State
Only that its aircraft are less than 20 years old

explanation: Before being granted an AOC, the operator must demonstrate that the operation is not only commercially viable but also safe.

question: Why may an operator from one contracting State plan to use an aerodrome in another contracting State without checking it further?

options.text: The operator must always inspect the aerodrome in person first
Aerodromes in every State are certified by a single world agency
States rely on each other's acceptance of the standards
Every aerodrome is inspected by the operator's own State

explanation: A general principle of accepting the international standards is that other States can rely on that acceptance without further verification. A State's compliance is sufficient evidence for a foreign operator to plan to use its aerodromes.

question: What is an alternate aerodrome?

options.text: Where an aircraft may go if it cannot or should not land as intended
Any aerodrome along the route with a runway long enough for the aircraft at its planned landing mass
An aerodrome kept open only for emergencies
The aerodrome from which the flight departs

explanation: An alternate aerodrome is one to which an aircraft may proceed when it becomes either impossible or inadvisable to proceed to, or land at, the aerodrome of intended landing.

question: What is a take-off alternate?

options.text: An aerodrome chosen in case the destination cannot be used
An aerodrome used en route after an engine failure
An aerodrome at which the aircraft can take off if the departure runway is closed
Where to land soon after take-off if departure is unusable

explanation: A take-off alternate is an aerodrome at which an aircraft can land if necessary shortly after take-off, when the aerodrome of departure cannot be used. It is chosen during planning on the day.

question: What is an en route alternate?

options.text: The aerodrome chosen before departure in case the destination is closed on arrival
Where to land after an en route abnormal or emergency
A military aerodrome along the route
An aerodrome used only in the climb after take-off

explanation: An en route alternate is an aerodrome at which an aircraft would be able to land after experiencing an abnormal or emergency condition en route.

question: What is an ETOPS en route alternate?

options.text: An aerodrome at the end of an oceanic track
An alternate used only by four-engine aircraft
A suitable aerodrome for a twin after an engine shutdown on an extended-range flight
The destination alternate of a long-range twin

explanation: An ETOPS en route alternate is a suitable and appropriate aerodrome at which an aeroplane could land after an engine shutdown or other abnormal or emergency condition en route on an extended twin-engine operation.

question: What must always be true of an aeroplane on an extended twin-engine (ETOPS) operation?

options.text: It must carry a third engine
It must stay within range of a suitable alternate
It must fly above FL290
It must carry enough fuel for two diversions one after the other

explanation: An ETOPS aeroplane must always be flying within range of a suitable alternate aerodrome.

question: What is a destination alternate?

options.text: Where to go if landing at the destination is impossible or unwise
An aerodrome chosen in case the aircraft must return shortly after take-off
An aerodrome along the route for an engine failure
The aerodrome of departure, used when the destination is closed

explanation: A destination alternate is an aerodrome to which an aircraft may proceed should it become impossible or inadvisable to land at the aerodrome of intended landing. It is chosen during pre-flight planning.

question: In an emergency, which aerodromes may be used as en route alternates?

options.text: Only aerodromes with a precision approach
Only aerodromes listed in the operations manual as en route alternates
Only aerodromes in the State of the Operator
Any suitable aerodrome

explanation: Normally "operationally acceptable" aerodromes are selected as en route alternates, but in an emergency any suitable aerodrome could be used.

question: For aeroplanes, how is flight time defined?

options.text: From the scheduled departure time to the scheduled arrival time
From the moment the wheels leave the ground until they touch down
From first movement for take-off until finally coming to rest
From engine start to engine shutdown

explanation: Flight time is the total time from the moment an aeroplane first moves for the purpose of taking off until the moment it finally comes to rest at the end of the flight. This is "block to block" time.

question: What everyday term means the same as flight time for aeroplanes?

options.text: Block to block time
Engine running time
Airborne time
Duty time

explanation: Flight time is synonymous with "block to block" or "chock to chock" time.

question: An aeroplane is pushed back and then taxies to a de-icing bay before taxiing to the runway. When does flight time start?

options.text: When the de-icing bay is reached and de-icing has finished
At first movement for the purpose of take-off
When the engines are started at the stand
When the aeroplane lifts off the runway

explanation: Flight time starts when the aeroplane first moves for the purpose of taking off. In everyday use, block time is counted from first movement under its own power after push-back towards the runway.

question: Why must flight time be legally defined?

options.text: Because it decides which State's law applies
Because the aircraft's insurance depends on it
Crew flight time limits are based on it
Because landing fees are calculated from it

explanation: An AOC requires a flight time limitation scheme for crews, so flight time must have a legal definition for the regulations to be applied.

question: What must the State of the Operator establish?

options.text: A safety management system inside each airline
A flight data analysis programme for each aircraft
An accident investigation board inside each airline, reporting to the State
A safety programme with an acceptable level of safety

explanation: The State establishes a safety programme with an acceptable level of safety; each operator establishes its own safety management system (SMS).

question: What must each operator establish throughout its operation?

options.text: A State safety programme
A safety management system (SMS)
A national aviation security programme
An accident investigation authority

explanation: The operator is required to establish a safety management system throughout the operation, to meet the level of safety defined by the State.

question: Which of these is a function of the operator's safety programme?

options.text: Identifying hazards and ensuring remedial action
Approving aircraft for the State's register
Investigating accidents on behalf of the State
Setting the national level of safety for all operators

explanation: The programme must identify safety hazards, ensure remedial action is implemented, provide continuous monitoring and assessment, and make continuous improvement of safety.

question: What is the purpose of the flight safety document system?

options.text: To record every flight for accident investigation
To store the maintenance records of each aircraft
To hold the personal training and licence records of each pilot for the authority
To list operations documents and how changes are notified

explanation: As part of the SMS, the operator establishes a flight safety document system that lists the documents used by operations personnel and how amendments are notified, ideally in a standard format and language.

question: Above what maximum certificated take-off mass must an operator have a flight data analysis programme?
explanation: An operator of aeroplanes with a maximum certificated take-off mass greater than 27 000 kg must establish a flight data analysis programme as part of its safety programme.

question: Who is responsible for determining that an aircraft used in commercial air transport is airworthy?

options.text: The operator
The air traffic control unit
The aircraft manufacturer
The State of Design

explanation: The operator is required to determine that any aircraft used in commercial air transport is airworthy. The commander checks the documents that show it.

question: What does a maintenance release certify?

options.text: That the aircraft has passed its annual certificate of airworthiness renewal
That the crew have completed their recurrent training
That the maintenance was done properly to approved data
That the aircraft has enough fuel for the flight

explanation: A maintenance release certifies that the maintenance work has been completed satisfactorily, in accordance with approved data and the maintenance organisation's procedures manual.

question: Which of these must a maintenance release contain?

options.text: The name of the commander for the next flight
The fuel uplift for the next flight
The number of passengers booked
Who signed the release

explanation: A maintenance release contains basic details of the work and the approved data used, the date of completion, the identity of the approved maintenance organisation and the identity of the person signing it.

question: Which lights are required by the rules of the air to be shown by aircraft?

options.text: Cabin lights and instrument lights
Navigation and anti-collision lights
Logo lights and wing inspection lights
Landing lights and taxi lights

explanation: The rules of the air cover navigation lights (showing the aircraft's course) and anti-collision lights. Landing, ice detection, instrument and cabin lights are not subject to statutory use.

question: What colour is the left (port) navigation light?

options.text: Amber
Green
White
Red

explanation: The port (left) light is red, the starboard (right) light green and the tail light white.

question: What colour is the right (starboard) navigation light?

options.text: Red
Blue
Green
White

explanation: The starboard (right) navigation light is green.

question: Through what horizontal angle does each wing-tip navigation light show?

options.text: 180° from dead ahead
110° from dead ahead
70° from dead ahead
90° from dead ahead

explanation: The port and starboard lights each show horizontally through 110° from dead ahead to their own side.

question: Through what total horizontal angle does the white tail navigation light show?

options.text: 140°, 70° each side of the axis
180°, 90° either side of the axis
220°, 110° either side of the fore-and-aft axis
110°, 55° either side of the axis

explanation: The tail light shows 70° either side of the plane of symmetry, a total of 140°. Together with the two 110° wing lights this covers the full 360°.

question: At night you see another aircraft at your level showing a red light on your right and a green light on your left. What is it doing?

options.text: Crossing from your right to your left
Flying away from you
Crossing from your left to your right
Flying towards you, head-on

explanation: An aircraft's red light is on its left and its green light on its right. When it faces you, its left is on your right, so red on your right and green on your left means it is coming towards you. From behind you would see only the white tail light.

question: Through what vertical angle do the wing-tip navigation lights show?
explanation: Vertically, the port and starboard lights show through 180°, the arc being towards their own side, so they can be seen from above and below.

question: What kind of light do most modern aeroplanes show as navigation lights?

options.text: A steady light at all times
Lights that alternate on and off independently
A light that flashes once a second
Lights that are switched on only in cloud

explanation: Most aeroplanes now show steady navigation lights. Some older aircraft have lights that alternate on and off together or independently.

question: Which two types of anti-collision light are in common use?

options.text: Landing lights and taxi lights
Rotating beacons and strobes
Steady red lights and steady green lights
Logo lights and wing inspection lights

explanation: Anti-collision lights may be of the rotating beacon type or the high-intensity strobe (capacitor discharge) type.
